title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: In a system built around a language model, "control flow" means the choice of which step runs next. Which statement correctly separates a workflow from an agent?

options.text: A workflow never calls tools, while an agent calls tools to get things done
A workflow never calls a model, while an agent calls a model at each step
In a workflow, the code fixes the step order; in an agent, the model chooses it
In a workflow, the model fixes the step order; in an agent, the code chooses it

items.stem: A student tells the makerspace assistant, "My 3D print keeps peeling off the bed." Nobody can say in advance which manual pages, checks or follow-up questions the answer will need. Which design fits this request best?

options.text: An agent, because the steps depend on what each tool result turns up
A fixed workflow, because any request that needs tools should be fixed
A fixed workflow, because a fixed order is always cheaper than a loop
An agent, because agents are always more reliable than fixed workflows

items.stem: Compared with a fixed workflow that does the same job, what does handing the control flow to an agent usually cost your team, and what does it buy?

options.text: It costs fewer model calls and buys a guarantee that each step happens
It costs more engineering time and buys a lower price for each request
It costs nothing extra and buys better answers on every kind of request
It costs more calls and less predictability, and buys flexibility on open tasks

items.stem: A student asks, "Is the laser cutter free tomorrow at 3 pm, and do I need training to use it?" As a fixed workflow, the code makes one model call to label the question as a booking question, then runs check_calendar and check_training_record itself in that order, then makes one model call to write the answer. An agent handling the same question made 4 model calls. How many fewer model calls does the workflow make than the agent?
In one sentence, who decides what happens after a tool returns its result in a fixed workflow, and who decides it in an agent?

Booking a machine always goes the same way: check the student's training record, check the calendar, then write the booking. In one or two sentences, give a reason to build this part as a fixed workflow rather than an agent.
